claims.text: Fine-grained syntactic elements within a prompt, such as constraints, guards, conditions, and concept bindings, consistently affect the likelihood of an open LLM generating insecure code.
Minimal changes to a prompt, as small as a single character, can cause an LLM to switch from generating secure code to vulnerable code.
The position of syntactic elements within a prompt also influences the security of the code generated by an LLM.

One study found that various prompt engineering methods, including a weaknesses-aware zero-shot chain-of-thought (WA-0CoT) strategy, failed to produce statistically significant reductions in overall vulnerability frequency or density.

While not reducing overall vulnerability counts, security-aware prompting strategies can systematically change the distribution of CWE vulnerability categories in the output, with effects varying by programming language.

Conditioning prompts with domain-specific terminology from critical infrastructure sectors does not create a statistically significant change in vulnerability rates compared to neutral baseline prompts.
One study suggests that prompt engineering alone is insufficient to reliably reduce overall vulnerability levels in LLM-generated code.
In contrast to prompt framing, the choice of LLM has a large and consistent effect on the rate of vulnerabilities in generated code.
A system called SecureForge can automatically optimize system prompts to reduce security vulnerabilities in LLM-generated code by up to 48%.
Even when explicitly prompted to write secure code and avoid specific weaknesses, frontier models still produced verifiable vulnerabilities in 23% of cases on average across a corpus of 250 prompts.

Analysis of model hidden states shows that input-handling vulnerabilities are more predictable from prompt representations (mean AUC 0.753) than vulnerabilities stemming from insecure default parameters (mean AUC 0.674).

A study investigated the impact of psychologically-inspired prompt framings on LLM code generation by operationalizing eight influence tactics, such as rational persuasion and ingratiation, into prompt templates.
In a study of influence tactics, code generated by LLMs was assessed on functional correctness, quality, maintainability, and security.
Prompt framings that emphasize urgency have been associated with reduced correctness and security in LLM-generated code.
While prompt engineering can alter the types of security weaknesses in LLM-generated code, it may not be sufficient on its own to reliably decrease the overall number of vulnerabilities.
Even minimal, single-character changes to prompts can cause an LLM to generate vulnerable code instead of secure code.
Specific syntactic elements in a prompt, such as constraints, guards, and conditions, and their placement can consistently affect the security of code generated by open LLMs.
A weaknesses-aware zero-shot chain-of-thought (WA-0CoT) prompting strategy enriches prompts with security context using Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) mappings to guide a model's reasoning.
An empirical evaluation of the WA-0CoT strategy found no statistically significant reductions in the frequency or density of vulnerabilities in the generated code.

While not reducing overall vulnerability levels, security-aware prompting strategies like WA-0CoT were found to systematically influence the distribution of different CWE vulnerability categories, with effects varying by programming language.
The Mitigation-Aware Chain-of-Thought (MA-CoT) framework is a prompting strategy that embeds task-specific CWE mitigation guidance and language-aware safeguards to reduce vulnerabilities.

In an evaluation using static analysis and expert validation, the MA-CoT framework reduced total security findings from 92 to 39 (a 57.6% reduction) on one dataset and from 73 to 4 (a 94.5% reduction) on the LLMSecEval benchmark.
The MA-CoT strategy was found to be the only one among those tested (Vanilla, Zero-shot, CoT, MA-CoT) that consistently improved security reliability.
Standard Zero-shot and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting strategies were found to be less reliable and may even increase vulnerabilities, particularly in the C programming language.
One study concludes that prompt engineering alone is insufficient to reliably reduce overall vulnerability levels in LLM-generated code.
A phenomenon known as "error propagation" occurs when faults in LLM-generated source code are systematically replicated in the test suites subsequently generated for that code.
Error propagation can result in situations where incorrect code and incorrect tests are mutually consistent, which serves to mask defects instead of exposing them.

An empirical study showed that generating tests after creating faulty code significantly diminishes fault detection effectiveness, dropping it to 14% compared to 25% when tests are generated independently.
The bias from erroneous code that influences subsequent test generation persists even under different prompting strategies, including chain-of-thought reasoning.

LLMs have been observed to struggle with maintaining functional correctness during multi-turn code refinement dialogues, with correctness dropping significantly for both open-weight and proprietary models.
In an evaluation of 16 models from five provider families on deterministic programming tasks, the effects of prompt templates were found to be model-dependent rather than uniformly beneficial.
The robustness of a large language model to prompt mutations is not a fixed property of the model but is highly dependent on the structure of the prompt.
The same prompt under-specification mutations that degrade performance on the HumanEval benchmark have a near-zero net effect on the structurally richer LiveCodeBench benchmark.

This inconsistency is because structurally rich task descriptions, like those in LiveCodeBench, can mitigate the negative effects of under-specification through redundancy in descriptions, constraints, and examples.
In a study of five open-weight LLMs, prompt framings that emphasized urgency were associated with reduced correctness and security in code generation tasks.
Different prompt wordings for the same coding task can cause a coding agent to perform vastly different kinds and amounts of work, even when producing the same correct patch.
Prompts that encourage "multiple approaches" and "deep thinking" primarily inflate the reasoning effort of a coding agent.

Requesting "multiple approaches" in a prompt can increase an agent's reasoning effort by 2.4x to 7.4x and cause it to generate multiple discarded solution branches, without improving the final success rate.
Prompts that ask for "maximum certainty" can trigger a pattern of repeated verification, leading to extra test runs, tool calls, turns, latency, and context growth.
Agent runs with high levels of redundant verification can cost 18 times the median, execute 2.5 times more tool calls, and take 3 times longer, without a corresponding increase in success.
Wasted work from prompts can be categorized into distinct types: some prompts are "reasoning-heavy and token-borne," while others are "tool-heavy and system-borne."
Using "bounded-efficiency" wording in prompts can avoid measured waste mechanisms while preserving necessary diagnosis and final validation steps.
The performance and cost effects of prompts interact with decoding settings, and the optimal configuration of model, prompt, and decoding settings varies with task difficulty.

A difficulty-aware method that jointly optimizes over models, prompts, and decoding settings can significantly reduce cost while improving success rates compared to using a single fixed configuration.
Rather than eliminating flaws, AI-generated software introduces a distinct 'machine signature of defects'.
A 'Reasoning-Complexity Trade-off' has been observed, where more capable models generate increasingly bloated and coupled code.
LLMs can amplify traditional forms of technical debt, such as code, design, and documentation debt.

Projects generated entirely by LLMs (PureAI) may show lower code smell density but also oversimplification, missing abstractions, and weaker responsibility separation compared to human-developed projects.
A 'Volume-Quality Inverse Law' has been proposed, where the volume of AI-generated code is a near-perfect predictor of its structural degradation.
New categories of LLM-specific debt have been identified, including prompt, ethical, data, and provenance debt.
The architectural decay in AI-generated code is not mitigated by achieving functional correctness or using detailed prompts.
'Fast-integration debt' is an emerging form of technical debt where rapidly generated code prioritizes speed over quality, leading to higher long-term maintenance costs.
Human-involved software projects created after the widespread use of LLMs show tendencies toward oversimplification, making them more similar to purely AI-generated projects.
A proxy analysis of code repositories suggests that code likely generated by LLMs exhibits substantial intra-repository code clones.
There are currently no standardized benchmarks or LLM-specific metrics to measure the technical debt introduced by these models.
A detector-based proxy analysis found that only a small percentage of human-labeled bugs are likely associated with LLM-generated code.
The central challenge in AI-based software engineering is shifting from code generation to managing architectural complexity.
In a study of developer-ChatGPT interactions in open-source pull requests, prompt structure was analyzed using three dimensions: Context, Specificity, and Verification.
Prompt characteristics have distinct, stage-dependent effects on AI-assisted software engineering workflows, influencing downstream code adoption and integration.
The prompt dimensions of Specificity and Context are most strongly associated with the generation of actionable code.
Verification within a prompt is the primary predictor of whether a developer will adopt the LLM-generated code.
The integration depth of LLM-generated code in a pull request is most strongly associated with the amount of Context provided in the prompt.
Prompt design elements like including a function signature, constraints, and style descriptions are most strongly associated with the readability of code generated by LLMs.
Using psychologically-based influence tactics in prompts, such as emphasizing urgency, can result in reduced correctness and security of the generated code.
Prompt engineering is a strategy suggested in the literature for mitigating the technical debt that LLM-assisted development can introduce.
The readability of code generated by LLMs is most strongly associated with prompts that include the function signature, constraints, and a description of the desired style.
Using psychologically-inspired prompt framings that emphasize urgency has been associated with reduced functional correctness and security in LLM-generated code.

Different aspects of prompt structure influence different stages of the development workflow; prompt specificity and context are most associated with generating actionable code, while verification cues are the primary predictor of code adoption.
The rapid generation of code can create "fast-integration debt," where speed is prioritized over quality, leading to a domino effect that increases long-term maintenance costs.
The depth of integration for LLM-generated code within a project is most strongly associated with the amount of context provided in the prompt.
Evaluations using various prompting strategies show that LLMs still struggle with harder problems and can make fundamental errors, impacting the functional correctness of the generated code.
LLM adoption introduces new categories of technical debt, including "prompt debt," which is unique to the challenges of using LLMs in software development.
Reasoning models consistently improve their code over multiple iterations and substantially outperform non-reasoning models in leveraging feedback from compiler errors and test cases.
For reasoning models, the wording of a prompt can dramatically change the type and amount of work performed, even when the requested code change and final correct output are the same.
Prompting a reasoning model to consider "multiple approaches" can increase the amount of reasoning work by 2.4x to 7.4x without yielding any gain in the task's success rate.
Prompts that ask for "maximum certainty" can cause reasoning models to engage in redundant verification, increasing tool calls by 2.5x and latency by 3x, again without improving success.
Using "bounded-efficiency wording" in prompts for reasoning agents can preserve diagnosis and validation steps while avoiding wasteful work mechanisms.
The effects of different prompt templates on code generation are model-dependent rather than being uniformly beneficial across all systems.
While prompt elements like function signature, constraints, and style descriptions are associated with code readability, the overall role of prompt design in improving readability is bounded.
In iterative feedback loops, syntactic and runtime errors are significantly more tractable for LLMs to correct than logical or algorithmic failures.

The wording of a prompt can determine where a coding agent spends its effort, leading to different cost structures; some prompts are reasoning-heavy and token-borne, while others are tool-heavy and system-borne.

Prompting a coding agent to consider "multiple approaches" can inflate reasoning effort by 2.4x to 7.4x and generate several discarded solutions, all without any improvement in the final success rate.

Prompts designed to elicit "maximum certainty" can trigger repeated verification steps, increasing run costs by a factor of 18, tool calls by 2.5x, and latency by 3x, also without a corresponding increase in success.

It is possible to improve both defect rate and cost simultaneously; one method, COMPAS, improved code generation pass rates from 45.9% to 52.8% while cutting costs from $36.57 to $4.92 on the LiveCodeBench benchmark.
The optimal configuration of model, prompt, and decoding settings for code generation varies with task difficulty, suggesting that a single fixed configuration is suboptimal.
In the context of LLM-assisted pull requests, the 'Specificity' and 'Context' of a prompt are most strongly associated with the generation of actionable code.
The inclusion of 'Verification' cues within a prompt is the primary predictor of whether LLM-generated code is ultimately adopted in a software project.
The impact of different prompt templates on performance is not uniform but is instead model-dependent.
An alternative to wasteful prompting patterns is "bounded-efficiency" wording, which can preserve essential diagnosis and validation steps while avoiding unnecessary work.
The impact of a prompt's natural language on code quality varies depending on both the programming language (e.g., Python or Java) and the specific LLM used.

In a study of code generation for Python and Java, prompts written in English did not consistently produce the best results in terms of functional correctness or code quality compared to prompts in Chinese, Hindi, Spanish, and Italian.

Prompting strategies, including security-aware ones, can systematically influence the distribution of different categories of security weaknesses (CWEs) in generated code, with the effects varying by programming language.
An evaluation of LLM-generated code in Java, C++, C, and Python suggests that prompt design for evaluating security properties should be both language-aware and model-aware.
Smaller LLMs tend to struggle more with programming languages that have fewer available training resources.
In a study of developer-ChatGPT interactions within open-source pull requests, prompt structure was analyzed using the dimensions of Context, Specificity, and Verification.
Prompts with greater Specificity and Context were most strongly linked to the generation of actionable code.
The Verification dimension of a prompt, which includes cues for evaluating the output, was the main predictor of whether LLM-generated code was adopted by the developer.
The depth of the code's integration into a project was most strongly associated with the amount of Context provided in the prompt.
A tertiary review of the field concludes that while LLMs show strong accuracy on benchmarks, the generalization of these results to real-world development is weakly supported.
On benchmark tasks, using psychology-based influence tactics in prompts can affect code quality; for instance, prompts emphasizing urgency were associated with reduced correctness and security.
In a benchmark designed to mimic real-world development, generating an entire repository at once was the best strategy for smaller repositories.
For more complex repositories, a module-by-module generation strategy performed better than other strategies in a benchmark aligned with industry practices.
Even when provided with structured system designs like UML diagrams, the quality of LLM-generated modules is often poor due to grammar and logic errors.
In code generation, prompts and decoding settings have been observed to interact with each other.
The optimal configuration of model, prompt, and decoding settings for code generation varies depending on the difficulty of the programming task.
The effects of tuning prompts and decoding settings can differ depending on the specific large language model being used.
A method called COMPAS was developed to perform a joint search over models, prompts, and decoding settings, routing tasks to an optimal configuration based on difficulty.
The impact of different prompt templates on code generation accuracy is model-dependent and not uniformly beneficial across all systems.
Prompt structure and task complexity interact to affect code correctness, with under-specification sometimes improving correctness on structurally rich tasks by breaking misleading cues.
